Global infrastructure notes.

- A **Region** is a separate geographic area, designed to be isolated from the other Regions. They have codes
  like us-east-1 (N. Virginia) and eu-west-1 (Ireland).
- Most resources are **regional**: you pick a Region and you only see that Region's stuff. AWS doesn't copy
  things between Regions for you.
- Each Region has **at least three Availability Zones (AZs)**. An AZ is "one or more discrete data centers",
  each with redundant power, networking and connectivity, in separate facilities. AZs in a Region are linked
  by low-latency fibre and don't share single points of failure.
- AZ names are the Region code plus a letter, like us-east-2a. There's also an **AZ ID**, like use2-az1,
  which is the same physical AZ in every account.
- Three flavours of resource: **zonal** (lives in one AZ), **regional**, and **global** (not tied to any
  Region). For high availability you spread across several AZs. Which things are which, I'll learn as I meet
  them.
- Choosing a Region: latency (be close to your users), cost, compliance and data residency, and whether the
  service you need is offered there. Some Regions are opt-in.
- Scale right now: 39 Regions, 124 AZs, 750+ edge points of presence. Saudi Arabia and Chile are announced.
- Edge locations (points of presence) are a different kind of site, not Regions. The service that uses
  them isn't on our plan, so I stopped there. Local Zones and Wavelength Zones also exist; I only skimmed those.

retrieved.body:
Account day. Today was about the account itself and the scary all-powerful login.

- A new AWS account starts with exactly one identity: the **root user**. That's the email and password I
  signed up with, and it has complete access to every service and resource in the account.
- The account itself is identified by a 12-digit **account ID**.
- Rule number one: don't use root for everyday work. Save it for the root-only tasks, like changing the
  account's email or the root password, closing the account, and some billing and tax settings. What to use
  *instead* for daily work, I don't know yet. I'm guessing the IAM days get into it somehow?
- **MFA on root is required now**, for every kind of account. You have to register it within 35 days of your
  first console sign-in attempt.
- Supported MFA types:
  - passkeys and security keys (FIDO), which AWS recommends
  - virtual authenticator apps (the 6-digit TOTP codes)
  - hardware TOTP tokens
- Lots of older tutorials still say MFA on root is "recommended". That's out of date: it's required.
- My plan: passkey on the root user, write down where the recovery stuff lives, and then basically never
  touch root again.
shaky: 'Root user' vs 'root' on Linux or a rooted phone: same word, and I'm not sure how far the 'full control' comparison really goes.
If root can do everything, can anything restrict it at all? For a standalone account like ours it sounds like basically no, which is exactly why MFA is required.

retrieved.body:
Billing, because I really don't want a surprise bill.

- The Free Tier changed for accounts created on or after **July 15, 2025**: USD 100 in credits at sign-up,
  plus up to USD 100 more for completing some starter activities (setting up a budget is one of them). Over
  30 services are always free.
- At sign-up you pick a plan:
  - **Free plan**: no charges at all. It ends after 6 months or when the credits run out, whichever comes
    first. Then the account *closes*. AWS keeps your content for 90 days, and you can upgrade to Paid in that
    window.
  - **Paid plan**: all services, pay-as-you-go once the credits are gone.
- Accounts from before July 15, 2025 keep the old model (12 months free, always-free, trials). So a lot of
  tutorials are describing the legacy setup.
- **AWS Budgets**: set a cost or usage budget and get alerts (email) on actual and *forecasted* spend. Budget
  data updates up to 3 times a day, so alerts lag behind real spend.
- **Cost Explorer**: look back up to 13 months and forecast 12 months ahead.
- **AWS Pricing Calculator**: estimate costs before building anything.
- Stuff I set up in a Region I'm not looking at is easy to forget about. Check all of them.
shaky: A budget alert isn't a spending cap. It notifies me (and apparently can trigger actions) but doesn't stop spend by itself, and it's delayed. So what actually stops a runaway bill? Me, I guess.
On the Free plan you 'can't be charged', but the account closes after 6 months unless you upgrade. I did not expect that.
Tutorials saying '12 months free' are only right for legacy accounts, I think. I need to check which kind we're on.

- AWS does security **of** the cloud: the hardware, the buildings, the network, and the virtualization layer
  everything runs on.

IAM policies: the anatomy. Dense day.

- A policy is a (mostly JSON) document that defines permissions when it's attached to an identity or a
  resource. AWS checks policies on *every* request, whether it came from the console, CLI or API.
- The one I wrote to learn it, letting a user change their own password:

  ```
  {
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [{
      "Sid": "SelfPassword",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "iam:ChangePassword",
      "Resource": "*"
    }]
  }
  ```
- Elements: `Version` (always `2012-10-17`), `Statement` (one or more), optional `Sid`, `Effect`
  (`Allow` or `Deny`), `Action`, `Resource`, optional `Condition` (e.g. `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` to
  require MFA).
- Actions look like `service:Action`, and wildcards work, e.g. `iam:*AccessKey*`.
- Resources are **ARNs**: `arn:aws:service:region:account:resource` (for normal accounts the first part is
  just `aws`). IAM ARNs leave the Region blank:
  `arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/Bob`.
- `Principal` only shows up in **resource-based** policies. In identity-based ones the principal is implied:
  it's whoever the policy is attached to.
- Identity-based policies attach to users and groups (roles too, day 6) and come in three kinds:
  - **AWS managed**: written by AWS, shared by everyone
  - **customer managed**: mine, reusable, keeps up to 5 versions
  - **inline**: embedded in one identity, deleted along with it
- Resource-based policies attach to a resource instead, must name a `Principal`, and are always inline. I
  haven't met a real one yet.
- Size limits: managed policy 6,144 characters; inline 2,048 per user, 5,120 per group (whitespace doesn't
  count).
- The console has a visual editor, so I don't *have* to hand-write JSON.

How AWS decides allow vs deny, and least privilege.

- Order: authenticate the principal, build the request context, then evaluate every policy that applies.
- Default is **implicit deny**: if nothing allows it, it's denied.
- An **explicit Deny** in any policy beats every Allow. No exceptions.
- Allows from several statements or policies add up (they're OR-ed). Within one account, identity-based and
  resource-based allows form a union: either one can allow.
- Some policy types, like permissions boundaries, only **limit** and never grant. The effective permission is
  the overlap. Awareness only for now.
- A denied request shows up as `AccessDenied` / "not authorized to perform".
- **Least privilege** in practice: start with AWS managed policies, then tighten with customer managed ones.
- Tools for tightening:
  - **IAM Access Analyzer**: 100+ policy validation checks, can generate a policy from actual activity, and
    gives findings for access from the public or from
    outside the account. External-access analysis is free; unused-access
    analysis and custom policy checks cost extra.
  - last-accessed information, to see what's never used
- Policy summaries group actions into access levels: List, Read, Write, Permissions management, Tagging.

Account day. Today was about the account itself and the scary all-powerful login.

- A new AWS account starts with exactly one identity: the **root user**. That's the email and password I

- Rule number one: don't use root for everyday work. Save it for the root-only tasks, like changing the

  *instead* for daily work, I don't know yet. I'm guessing the IAM days get into it somehow?

  first console sign-in attempt.

  - hardware TOTP tokens

  touch root again.

Shared responsibility model: who secures what.

- AWS does security **of** the cloud: the hardware, the buildings, the network, and the virtualization layer
  everything runs on.
- I do security **in** the cloud: my data, who gets access to what, the operating system and apps on any
  machines I rent, and how I configure the services I use.
- The split moves depending on the kind of service. With raw infrastructure (IaaS), where I'm basically
  renting a machine, I'm patching its guest OS and my apps. With more managed, abstracted services AWS takes
  on more, and I'm mostly left with my data, how it's classified, and who can reach it. PaaS and SaaS push
  even more onto the provider.
- Three control types:
  - **inherited**: AWS does it and I just inherit it (physical security of the data centres)
  - **shared**: we each do our own layer (patch management, configuration management, awareness and
    training)
  - **customer-specific**: entirely mine
- Takeaway: AWS gives me safe building blocks, but if I set something up badly, that's on me, not them.

- IAM = AWS Identity and Access Management. It controls who is **authenticated** (signed in) and

  actually does yet.
- IAM is **eventually consistent**: a change can take a moment to propagate, so the docs say keep IAM changes

Shared responsibility model: who secures what.

- AWS does security **of** the cloud: the hardware, the buildings, the network, and the virtualization layer
  everything runs on.
- I do security **in** the cloud: my data, who gets access to what, the operating system and apps on any
  machines I rent, and how I configure the services I use.
- The split moves depending on the kind of service. With raw infrastructure (IaaS), where I'm basically
  renting a machine, I'm patching its guest OS and my apps. With more managed, abstracted services AWS takes
  on more, and I'm mostly left with my data, how it's classified, and who can reach it. PaaS and SaaS push
  even more onto the provider.
- Three control types:
  - **inherited**: AWS does it and I just inherit it (physical security of the data centres)
  - **shared**: we each do our own layer (patch management, configuration management, awareness and
    training)
  - **customer-specific**: entirely mine
- Takeaway: AWS gives me safe building blocks, but if I set something up badly, that's on me, not them.

Access keys and the CLI.

- **Access keys** are for programmatic access (CLI, SDKs, APIs). A key is two parts:
  - an **access key ID**, like `AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE` (`AKIA` = long-term key)
  - a **secret access key**
- The secret is shown **only once**, when you create the key. Lose it and you make a new key.
- Max **2** access keys per user, so you can rotate: make the new one, switch over, delete the old one.
- Never create access keys for the root user.
- Never put keys in code.
- `aws configure` is how I hand the CLI a key. It ends up in the shared credentials file,
  `~/.aws/credentials`, which is **plaintext**. That made me a bit nervous.
- Named **CLI profiles** let me keep separate sets of credentials side by side.
- Commands I tried reading about: `aws iam create-user`, `aws iam create-group`,
  `aws iam add-user-to-group`, `aws iam create-access-key` (API names `CreateUser`, `CreateAccessKey`).

retrieved.body:
IAM users and groups.

- An **IAM user** is an identity inside my account for one person or one application. It has **long-term
  credentials**: a console password, access keys, or both.
- Up to 5,000 users per account. Names are case-insensitive for uniqueness, so I can't have both `ADMINS`
  and `admins`.
- **User groups** are collections of users. Give the group permissions once and every member gets them. (The
  permission documents themselves are day 5.)
  - a user can be in up to 10 groups
  - groups **can't be nested**
  - there's **no default "all users" group**
  - 300 groups per account by default (adjustable)
- MFA can be turned on per IAM user, up to 8 MFA devices each. Same as yesterday's root advice:
  phishing-resistant passkeys or security keys are preferred.
- Every user and group gets a unique ID behind the scenes with a telltale start: `AIDA` = user,
  `AGPA` = group.
- **Credential report**: lists all users and the state of their credentials. Handy for catching old passwords
  and keys nobody uses.
- Twist: AWS now says IAM users are *not* the recommended way for humans to sign in. They're meant for cases
  like third-party tools and emergency access. The docs point somewhere else for humans; I haven't followed
  that thread yet.
shaky: Every tutorial says 'make an IAM admin user for daily use', but current AWS guidance says IAM users aren't the recommended way for people. For just the two of us on one personal account, is an IAM user fine? Genuinely unsure.
So a group is basically just a way to hand the same permissions to several users? No nesting feels limiting, I don't get why.

How AWS decides allow vs deny, and least privilege.

- Order: authenticate the principal, build the request context, then evaluate every policy that applies.
- Default is **implicit deny**: if nothing allows it, it's denied.
- An **explicit Deny** in any policy beats every Allow. No exceptions.
- Allows from several statements or policies add up (they're OR-ed). Within one account, identity-based and
  resource-based allows form a union: either one can allow.
- Some policy types, like permissions boundaries, only **limit** and never grant. The effective permission is
  the overlap. Awareness only for now.
- A denied request shows up as `AccessDenied` / "not authorized to perform".
- **Least privilege** in practice: start with AWS managed policies, then tighten with customer managed ones.
- Tools for tightening:
  - **IAM Access Analyzer**: 100+ policy validation checks, can generate a policy from actual activity, and
    gives findings for access from the public or from
    outside the account. External-access analysis is free; unused-access
    analysis and custom policy checks cost extra.
  - last-accessed information, to see what's never used
- Policy summaries group actions into access levels: List, Read, Write, Permissions management, Tagging.

Shared responsibility model: who secures what.

- AWS does security **of** the cloud: the hardware, the buildings, the network, and the virtualization layer
  everything runs on.
- I do security **in** the cloud: my data, who gets access to what, the operating system and apps on any
  machines I rent, and how I configure the services I use.
- The split moves depending on the kind of service. With raw infrastructure (IaaS), where I'm basically
  renting a machine, I'm patching its guest OS and my apps. With more managed, abstracted services AWS takes
  on more, and I'm mostly left with my data, how it's classified, and who can reach it. PaaS and SaaS push
  even more onto the provider.
- Three control types:
  - **inherited**: AWS does it and I just inherit it (physical security of the data centres)
  - **shared**: we each do our own layer (patch management, configuration management, awareness and
    training)
  - **customer-specific**: entirely mine
- Takeaway: AWS gives me safe building blocks, but if I set something up badly, that's on me, not them.

Access keys and the CLI.

- **Access keys** are for programmatic access (CLI, SDKs, APIs). A key is two parts:
  - an **access key ID**, like `AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE` (`AKIA` = long-term key)

- Never put keys in code.

- A new AWS account starts with exactly one identity: the **root user**. That's the email and password I

  - hardware TOTP tokens

IAM users and groups.

- An **IAM user** is an identity inside my account for one person or one application. It has **long-term
  credentials**: a console password, access keys, or both.
- Up to 5,000 users per account. Names are case-insensitive for uniqueness, so I can't have both `ADMINS`
  and `admins`.
- **User groups** are collections of users. Give the group permissions once and every member gets them. (The
  permission documents themselves are day 5.)
  - a user can be in up to 10 groups
  - groups **can't be nested**
  - there's **no default "all users" group**
  - 300 groups per account by default (adjustable)
- MFA can be turned on per IAM user, up to 8 MFA devices each. Same as yesterday's root advice:
  phishing-resistant passkeys or security keys are preferred.
- Every user and group gets a unique ID behind the scenes with a telltale start: `AIDA` = user,
  `AGPA` = group.
- **Credential report**: lists all users and the state of their credentials. Handy for catching old passwords
  and keys nobody uses.
- Twist: AWS now says IAM users are *not* the recommended way for humans to sign in. They're meant for cases
  like third-party tools and emergency access. The docs point somewhere else for humans; I haven't followed
  that thread yet.

S3 part 2: names, limits, consistency, CLI.

Bucket naming rules:
- 3 to 63 characters; lowercase letters, digits, dots and hyphens; must start and end with a letter or digit.
- Can't look like an IP address. Some reserved prefixes/suffixes, e.g. `xn--`, `sthree-`, `-s3alias`.
- The docs say avoid dots in names. Something about secure-connection addressing breaking; didn't fully dig in.
- Names are unique across ALL accounts in a partition (there are four partitions: aws, aws-cn, aws-us-gov and
  aws-eusc, the European Sovereign Cloud). So "my-bucket" is long gone.
- New since March 2026: the account regional namespace. Names end in `-<12-digit account ID>-<region>-an`
  and only have to be unique inside my account and Region.
- Creepy one: if I delete a bucket in the global namespace, someone else can create the same name and receive
  requests meant for me. AWS suggests emptying it and keeping it instead.

Sizes:
- An object can be 0 B up to 50 TB (it was 5 TB until Dec 2025).
- One single PUT upload tops out at 5 GB; the console upload at 160 GB. Beyond that it's multipart upload
  (the file goes up in parts, 10,000 parts max).

Consistency: strong read-after-write for PUT, DELETE and LIST of objects in every Region, since Dec 2020.
Write something, read it right back, I get the new thing. Two writers at once: last writer wins, no locking.
Bucket *configuration* changes are still eventually consistent though.

Durability: designed for 99.999999999% (11 nines), i.e. S3 basically doesn't lose data. Durability isn't the
same as availability (being reachable right now) and I need to keep those two apart.

CLI, high-level: `aws s3 mb s3://name`, `aws s3 cp`, `aws s3 ls`, `aws s3 sync`, `aws s3 rm`, `aws s3 rb`.
Low-level: `aws s3api create-bucket` etc. Outside us-east-1 you have to pass a LocationConstraint.

Lots of older posts still say S3 is 'eventually consistent'. It isn't for objects anymore, only bucket config. Easy to mix up.

Day 7, finally S3 (Simple Storage Service). It's *object storage*: I don't get a disk with a file system,
I get buckets and I put objects in them.

- Object = the data itself + metadata. Some metadata is system stuff (Content-Type, size, ETag), and I can
  add my own as x-amz-meta-something headers.
- Key = the object's unique name inside its bucket, e.g. `photos/puppy.jpg`. Bucket + key identifies an object.
- Keys can be up to 1,024 bytes long.

Folders are fake! The namespace is flat. `photos/` is just a prefix that a bunch of keys happen to share, and
the console draws it as a folder to be friendly. Clicking "Create folder" actually makes a 0-byte object whose
key ends in `/`. Kind of funny.

Compared with a normal hard drive: there I can rename a file, append to it, edit the middle. In S3 an object
is replaced as a whole. "Rename" is really copy to a new key + delete the old one. No appending.

Buckets:
- I create a bucket in a Region I pick. Its name and Region can't be changed afterwards, and the data stays in
  that Region unless I copy it somewhere else.
- No buckets inside buckets. No limit on how many objects a bucket holds or how big it gets.
- 10,000 buckets per account by default (older tutorials say 100, that's stale).
- There are four bucket types now: the normal one, plus directory, table and vector buckets. The docs
  say a beginner only needs the normal one, so I ignored the other three.

An object's URL looks like `https://my-bucket.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/photos/puppy.jpg`. ARNs (day 5 stuff)
look like `arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket` for the bucket and `arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/photos/puppy.jpg` for one object.

Who can actually read my objects? They're private unless access is granted somehow, and that's tomorrow's
topic (day 8, S3 access control), so I stopped there.
shaky: S3 is not a file system and I keep forgetting it. No real folders, no rename, no append. My brain still pictures a hard drive.
The console shows buckets from every Region in one list, yet each bucket lives in exactly one Region. That tripped me up for a minute.

Shared responsibility model: who secures what.

- AWS does security **of** the cloud: the hardware, the buildings, the network, and the virtualization layer
  everything runs on.
- I do security **in** the cloud: my data, who gets access to what, the operating system and apps on any
  machines I rent, and how I configure the services I use.
- The split moves depending on the kind of service. With raw infrastructure (IaaS), where I'm basically
  renting a machine, I'm patching its guest OS and my apps. With more managed, abstracted services AWS takes
  on more, and I'm mostly left with my data, how it's classified, and who can reach it. PaaS and SaaS push
  even more onto the provider.
- Three control types:
  - **inherited**: AWS does it and I just inherit it (physical security of the data centres)
  - **shared**: we each do our own layer (patch management, configuration management, awareness and
    training)
  - **customer-specific**: entirely mine
- Takeaway: AWS gives me safe building blocks, but if I set something up badly, that's on me, not them.

Shared responsibility model: who secures what.

- AWS does security **of** the cloud: the hardware, the buildings, the network, and the virtualization layer
  everything runs on.
- I do security **in** the cloud: my data, who gets access to what, the operating system and apps on any
  machines I rent, and how I configure the services I use.
- The split moves depending on the kind of service. With raw infrastructure (IaaS), where I'm basically
  renting a machine, I'm patching its guest OS and my apps. With more managed, abstracted services AWS takes
  on more, and I'm mostly left with my data, how it's classified, and who can reach it. PaaS and SaaS push
  even more onto the provider.
- Three control types:
  - **inherited**: AWS does it and I just inherit it (physical security of the data centres)
  - **shared**: we each do our own layer (patch management, configuration management, awareness and
    training)
  - **customer-specific**: entirely mine
- Takeaway: AWS gives me safe building blocks, but if I set something up badly, that's on me, not them.
shaky: 'AWS handles security' is wrong, since my misconfigurations are on me. But where exactly is the line for a given service? Sounds like I have to check service by service.
Patching: AWS patches the host underneath, I patch the guest OS on anything I rent. Host vs guest keeps tripping me up.

IAM overview (the detailed IAM days are 4 to 6).

- IAM = AWS Identity and Access Management. It controls who is **authenticated** (signed in) and
  **authorized** (has permissions) to use resources.
- Authentication = proving who you are. Authorization = what you're allowed to do once you're in.
- A **principal** is anything that can make a request to AWS. The root user from yesterday is one.
- IAM identities come as users, groups and roles. Users and groups are day 4, roles are day 6.
- New identities start with **no permissions** until someone grants them. **Least privilege** means granting
  only what a task actually needs. How permissions get written down is day 5.
- IAM is **global**: it isn't tied to a Region.
- IAM, Identity Center and STS (AWS Security Token Service) cost nothing extra. I haven't dug into what STS
  actually does yet.
- IAM is **eventually consistent**: a change can take a moment to propagate, so the docs say keep IAM changes
  out of critical, time-sensitive code paths.
- Handy: `aws sts get-caller-identity` tells me who AWS thinks I am right now.
shaky: AuthN vs AuthZ: I swap them constantly. N for who you are, Z for what you can do? My mnemonic is weak.
Eventual consistency: if I add a permission and immediately get denied, I might just need to wait? That feels odd for a security system.

Day 1! Today I learned what AWS actually is, beyond "Amazon's cloud".

- AWS rents out computing resources (servers, storage, databases and a lot more) and you pay for what you
  use, pay-as-you-go, instead of buying hardware up front. The docs also keep saying "elasticity": scale up
  when you need more, scale back down when you don't.
- Every capability is its own **service** with its own name. Signing up gives you access to all of them, and
  you're only charged for what you actually use. Names on our roadmap: IAM (days 3 to 6), S3 (from day 7),
  EC2 (from day 11). I don't know what they do yet, just that they're coming.
- Four ways to talk to AWS:
  1. the **AWS Management Console** (the website)
  2. the **AWS CLI** (command line)
  3. **SDKs** (code libraries; boto3 is the Python one)
  4. the raw **HTTP APIs**
- Big realisation: the console itself calls the same APIs. They're all different front-ends to the same
  thing, not different products.
- Every request to AWS gets signed (Signature Version 4, "SigV4") so AWS can tell who sent it, unless the
  request is anonymous. The CLI and SDKs do the signing for me. What the signing actually uses is something I
  haven't got to yet.
- Deployment models: all-in cloud, on-premises (your own data centre), or hybrid (a mix of both).

Global infrastructure notes.

- A **Region** is a separate geographic area, designed to be isolated from the other Regions. They have codes
  like us-east-1 (N. Virginia) and eu-west-1 (Ireland).
- Most resources are **regional**: you pick a Region and you only see that Region's stuff. AWS doesn't copy
  things between Regions for you.
- Each Region has **at least three Availability Zones (AZs)**. An AZ is "one or more discrete data centers",
  each with redundant power, networking and connectivity, in separate facilities. AZs in a Region are linked
  by low-latency fibre and don't share single points of failure.
- AZ names are the Region code plus a letter, like us-east-2a. There's also an **AZ ID**, like use2-az1,
  which is the same physical AZ in every account.
- Three flavours of resource: **zonal** (lives in one AZ), **regional**, and **global** (not tied to any
  Region). For high availability you spread across several AZs. Which things are which, I'll learn as I meet
  them.
- Choosing a Region: latency (be close to your users), cost, compliance and data residency, and whether the
  service you need is offered there. Some Regions are opt-in.
- Scale right now: 39 Regions, 124 AZs, 750+ edge points of presence. Saudi Arabia and Chile are announced.
- Edge locations (points of presence) are a different kind of site, not Regions. The service that uses
  them isn't on our plan, so I stopped there. Local Zones and Wavelength Zones also exist; I only skimmed those.
shaky: An AZ is not the same as a data centre. One AZ can be several data centres, and I keep forgetting that.

us-east-1a in my account might not be the same physical AZ as us-east-1a in yours, but only for older accounts in the oldest Regions; accounts from Nov 2025 get the same mapping. So that's why AZ IDs exist?
Apparently when stuff 'disappears' in the console, it's usually just the wrong Region selected. I bet I'll do this at least once.
